items.prompt: State what is meant by a kibibyte.
items.canonical_answer: A kibibyte is 1024 bytes, named with the binary prefix kibi, which steps by 1024 rather than by 1000.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - 1024 bytes, a binary prefix that steps by 1024, not a decimal prefix of 1000.

items.prompt: Describe the difference between a kilobyte and a kibibyte.
items.canonical_answer: A kilobyte is named with the decimal prefix kilo and is exactly 1000 bytes, whereas a kibibyte is named with the binary prefix kibi and is 1024 bytes. Both measure storage in bytes, but the decimal family steps by 1000 and the binary family steps by 1024, so the kibibyte is the larger of the two.
marking_guidance: Difference: a kilobyte is 1000 bytes with the decimal prefix kilo, whereas a kibibyte is 1024 bytes with the binary prefix kibi - 1 mark for each side, and both sides are needed.

items.prompt: One phone lists a photo as 2.4 MB and another phone lists the same photo as 2.3 MiB. Explain why the two figures differ even though the file is the same.
items.canonical_answer: The first phone counts the photo in decimal megabytes, so 2.4 MB means about 2.40 million bytes. The second counts it in binary mebibytes, so 2.3 MiB means about 2.41 million bytes, because one mebibyte holds 1,048,576 bytes against the megabyte's 1,000,000. The two phones describe the same file with two prefix families, so the numbers differ while the byte count is the same.
marking_guidance: Context: this phone counts with the decimal prefix mega while the other counts with the binary prefix mebi - 1 mark.
Reason: because the decimal family steps by 1000 and the binary family by 1024, the same file is described by two different numbers - 1 mark.

objective_titles: Show understanding of binary magnitudes and the difference between binary prefixes and decimal prefixes

items.prompt: A learner writes that a tebibyte is 1024 gigabytes. Explain the error and give the correct statement.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has joined the binary prefix tebi to the decimal unit gigabyte. A prefix containing "bi" is a binary prefix, so its steps of 1024 run through binary-prefixed units: one tebibyte is 1024 gibibytes, not 1024 gigabytes. The test is to check the unit as well as the step: a binary prefix steps by 1024 from one binary-prefixed unit to the next.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the binary step 1024 has been attached to the decimal unit gigabyte instead of the binary unit gibibyte, a confusion of the two prefix families.
1 mark: the correction with the test - a prefix containing "bi" steps by 1024 through binary-prefixed units, so 1 tebibyte is 1024 gibibytes.

objective_titles: Show understanding of binary magnitudes and the difference between binary prefixes and decimal prefixes

items.prompt: Describe two features of the binary prefixes.
items.canonical_answer: Each binary prefix contains the letters "bi" in its name, so the family is written kibi, mebi, gibi, tebi and its symbols carry a lower-case i, as in KiB and MiB. Each binary prefix steps by 1024 of the next smaller binary-prefixed unit: one kibibyte is 1024 bytes, one mebibyte is 1024 kibibytes, one gibibyte is 1024 mebibytes.
marking_guidance: Features: 1 mark per point - the "bi" naming with the lower-case i in the symbol, and the step of 1024 between consecutive binary-prefixed units. Two points, 1 mark each.

items.prompt: Explain why a memory card labelled 64 GB holds less than 64 GiB.
items.canonical_answer: The label uses the decimal prefix giga, so the card holds 64 thousand million bytes. A gibibyte counts 1024 mebibytes, and each mebibyte is 1,048,576 bytes, so 64 GiB counts more than 64 thousand million bytes. The decimal-labelled card therefore holds fewer bytes than 64 GiB, because the two labels come from the two prefix families and the binary one counts a larger byte total.
marking_guidance: Reason: the label uses the decimal prefix giga, counting 64 thousand million bytes - 1 mark.
Because the binary prefix family steps by 1024, a gibibyte counts more bytes than a gigabyte, so the card falls short of 64 GiB - 1 mark.

items.prompt: State the base of the hexadecimal number system and what a digit of it can be worth.
items.canonical_answer: Hexadecimal is base sixteen: each place value is a power of sixteen, and a single digit is worth 0 to 15, written 0 to 9 and A to F.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - base sixteen, with place values that are powers of 16 and digit values from 0 to 15 written 0-9 and A-F.

items.prompt: Convert the denary number 217 into hexadecimal.
items.canonical_answer: Sixteen goes into 217 thirteen times with 9 left, because 13 sixteens are 208 and 208 with 9 more is 217. Thirteen is written D and nine as 9, so 217 in hexadecimal is D9.
marking_guidance: Working: the method shown - division by sixteen with the remainder found (13 sixteens are 208, and 208 with 9 more is 217) - 1 mark.
Answer: D9, the final hexadecimal result.
Units: the result is a hexadecimal value, two digits.

items.prompt: Convert the binary pattern 1011 0110 into hexadecimal.
items.canonical_answer: Split the bits into groups of four from the right: 1011 and 0110. The group 1011 is eleven, written B, and the group 0110 is 6, so the pattern is B6 in hexadecimal.
marking_guidance: Working: the method shown - the bits split into two groups of four from the right, each group converted (1011 is 11, written B; 0110 is 6) - 1 mark.
Answer: B6, the final hexadecimal result.
Units: the result is a hexadecimal value.

items.prompt: Convert the denary number 49 into Binary Coded Decimal.
items.canonical_answer: BCD gives each denary digit its own 4-bit group: 4 is 0100 and 9 is 1001, so 49 in BCD is 0100 1001.
marking_guidance: Working: the method shown - each denary digit converted separately into its own 4-bit group (4 is 0100, 9 is 1001) - 1 mark.
Answer: 0100 1001, the final BCD result.

items.prompt: A weather station keeps a running season total of sunshine hours. The station stores the total as an 8-bit unsigned binary integer, shows it on a test screen in hexadecimal, and drives its digit display from a BCD store. items.prompt: Asked to write denary 46 in BCD, a learner answers 0010 1110. Explain the mistake and give the correct answer.
items.canonical_answer: The learner converted the whole number to pure binary, which gives 0010 1110. BCD instead stores each denary digit as its own 4-bit group: 4 is 0100 and 6 is 0110, so 46 in BCD is 0100 0110. The test is to count the digits: a BCD answer has one 4-bit group per denary digit, and no group is above 1001.

items.prompt: A register holds the 8-bit two's complement value 1001 1101. A learner reads it as +157. Explain the error and give the correct denary value.
items.canonical_answer: The learner read the most significant bit as +128, which treats the register as holding an unsigned value, so the minus sign was lost. In two's complement the most significant bit has the place value -128, so 1001 1101 is -128 with 16, 8, 4 and 1, which comes to -99. The test: when the leftmost bit is 1, a two's complement value must come out negative, so a positive answer means the leftmost bit was read as positive.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the value was read as unsigned, with the most significant bit taken as +128 instead of -128, so the minus sign was lost.
1 mark: the correction with the test - the value is -99, and a leftmost bit of 1 must give a negative answer in two's complement.

items.prompt: Asked to convert the hexadecimal value 7E into denary, a learner writes "7 and 14". Explain the error and give the correct denary value.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has written the digits' values side by side instead of using the place values. In 7E, the 7 sits in the sixteens column and the E, which is 14, sits in the units column, so the value is seven sixteens and fourteen units: 7 sixteens are 112, and 112 with 14 more is 126. The test: an answer that just joins the digit values has skipped the place values, so each digit must be multiplied by its power of sixteen and the results added.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the digits' denary values were joined side by side, instead of each digit being multiplied by its place value.
1 mark: the correction with the test - 7E is 126, found by multiplying each digit by its power of sixteen (7 sixteens are 112, and 112 with 14 more is 126).

items.prompt: Describe two features of two's complement representation.
items.canonical_answer: The most significant bit carries a negative place value, -128 in an 8-bit value, while every other bit keeps its positive place value, so the sign can be read straight from the leftmost bit. The 8-bit range runs from -128 to +127, with non-negative values beginning with a 0 bit and negative values beginning with a 1 bit.

items.prompt: Describe the difference between how pure binary and how BCD store the denary number 46.
items.canonical_answer: Pure binary converts the whole number with place values that are powers of two, so 46 is stored as the single 8-bit pattern 0010 1110. BCD keeps the denary digits instead: each digit gets its own 4-bit group, so 46 is stored as 0100 0110, one group for the 4 and one for the 6. Both store the same number, whereas the groups they store it in serve different jobs: pure binary is compact for arithmetic, BCD suits showing each denary digit separately.
marking_guidance: Difference: pure binary converts the whole value into one pattern (0010 1110), whereas BCD stores one 4-bit group per denary digit (0100 0110) - 1 mark for each side, and both sides are needed.

items.prompt: State what is meant by overflow in binary arithmetic.
items.canonical_answer: Overflow occurs when the result of a calculation needs more bits than the register holds, so the register keeps only part of the result and the stored value is wrong.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - a result that needs more bits than the register holds, so the stored value is not the true result.

items.prompt: Convert the denary integer -45 into its 8-bit two's complement binary value.
items.canonical_answer: Start from 45 as an 8-bit pattern: 0010 1101. Flip every bit: 1101 0010. Add 1, giving 1101 0010 + 1 = 1101 0011, which is the 8-bit two's complement form of -45. Checking the place values, -128 with 64, 16, 2 and 1 comes to -45.
marking_guidance: Working: the method shown - the bits of 45 flipped, then 1 added (1101 0010 + 1 = 1101 0011) - 1 mark.
Answer: 1101 0011, the final 8-bit result.
Units: the result is an 8-bit binary value in two's complement.

items.prompt:

items.prompt: A warehouse system in Gobabis counts bags of maize meal as an 8-bit unsigned binary integer. Yesterday it held 1100 0100 bags, and a delivery of 0110 1101 bags is added. Complete: (a) the true total in nine bits, (b) whether a carry into a ninth bit occurs, (c) whether overflow occurs in the 8-bit register, and (d) the 8-bit value the register then holds.
items.canonical_answer: (a) 1100 0100 + 0110 1101 = 1 0011 0001, so the true total in nine bits is 1 0011 0001. (b) A carry into a ninth bit does occur. (c) Overflow occurs in the 8-bit register, because the true total, 305, needs nine bits and the register holds eight. (d) The register keeps the low eight bits, 0011 0001, which is 49, so the system would record 49 bags instead of 305.
marking_guidance: Context: the warehouse system's 8-bit register with the given delivery totals - 1 mark per completed entry, (a) 1 0011 0001, (b) yes, (c) yes with the reason, (d) 0011 0001 which is 49.
Reason: each entry turns on the ninth bit - the true total needs more bits than the register holds, so overflow occurs and the stored value is wrong for the warehouse; the four entries carry 4 marks.

items.prompt: A technician reads the memory address 3F7 in a system's error log. Explain why the address is written in hexadecimal rather than binary.
items.canonical_answer: Each hexadecimal digit stands for exactly four bits, so 3F7 is a compact three-digit shorthand for the 12-bit pattern 0011 1111 0111. Writing the same address in binary takes four times as many characters, and one mis-read bit is easy to miss in a long string, so the hexadecimal form makes this log quicker for the technician to read and less error-prone.
marking_guidance: Context: this address, 3F7, in the error log - 1 mark.
Reason: because one hexadecimal digit maps to exactly four bits, the address is shorter to write and read than its 12-bit binary form, so errors are easier to avoid - 1 mark.

items.canonical_answer: Unicode allocates more bits per character than ASCII's 7, so it can represent many more characters, covering the world's writing systems rather than English letters, digits and punctuation alone. items.prompt: Describe the difference between ASCII and extended ASCII.
items.canonical_answer: ASCII is a 7-bit character set, so it defines 128 codes. Extended ASCII uses all 8 bits of a byte for each character, giving 256 codes. Both use the same codes for the first 128 characters, whereas extended ASCII adds codes 128 to 255, which is where accented and graphic characters are placed.

items.prompt:
The Etanga Craft Collective in Opuwo records basket sales on a small till. The till stores each day's count as an 8-bit unsigned binary integer, stores the seller's initials as ASCII characters, and labels the day's report file with its size in kilobytes.
(a) Identify the largest count the till's 8-bit field can hold. [1]
(b) The day's report file is labelled 40 kilobytes. State how many bytes the label counts. [1]
(c) On a busy day the stored count is 1111 1101 and a further 8 baskets are sold. Explain what happens in the 8-bit field when the 8 baskets are added, and what the till then records. [3]
(d) Explain why the initials stored with ASCII take 7 bits per character, and why the same stored bits could be read as different characters by a system that used a different character set. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The largest 8-bit unsigned value is 1111 1111, which is 255.
(b) The label counts 40,000 bytes, because kilo is a decimal prefix that steps by 1000.
(c) The addition 1111 1101 + 0000 1000 gives 1 0000 0101: the true total is 261, which needs a ninth bit, so the 8-bit field cannot hold it. Overflow occurs, the ninth bit is lost, and the till records 0000 0101, which is 5 baskets instead of 261.
(d) ASCII allocates 7 bits per character, so each initial is stored as a 7-bit code, giving 128 possible codes. The stored bits are simply the binary form of the code the set assigns, so a system reading those same bits against a different set could assign them different characters.
marking_guidance: Part (a): identify the largest value, 255 - 1 point.
Part (b): state 40,000 bytes, because kilo steps by 1000 as a decimal prefix - 1 point.

Part (c): the reason the till fails - the sum needs a ninth bit, so overflow occurs in the given system and the recorded value is wrong; 3 points: the 9-bit total, the overflow named with the reason, and the value recorded.

Part (d): the context of this scenario - ASCII's 7-bit allocation, and the same bits reading differently under a different set; 3 points: the 7-bit allocation, the code-as-bits principle, and the set-dependent reading.

items.prompt:
A community centre's entry system was tested with one number, 91. The table shows how three parts of the system stored it. Read the table and answer the questions.

| Part of the system | Stored form | Representation |
|---|---|---|
| Visitor counter (8-bit) | 0101 1011 | unsigned binary |
| Report header | 5B | hexadecimal |
| Digit display | (a) | BCD |

(b) In a busy month the counter adds 111 to the stored 91. Complete the 8-bit result of 0101 1011 + 0110 1111, and state, with a reason, whether overflow occurs in the 8-bit counter. [3]
(c) State the denary value of the report header 5B. [1]
(d) State why the digit display is driven from the BCD store rather than from the binary counter. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) In BCD each denary digit has its own 4-bit group: 9 is 1001 and 1 is 0001, so the display store is 1001 0001.
(b) 0101 1011 + 0110 1111 = 1100 1010, because 91 with 111 more is 202, and 202 fits in eight bits (a 128, a 64, an 8 and a 2). No carry into a ninth bit occurs, so no overflow occurs: the true total fits the register.
(c) 5B is five sixteens and eleven units: 5 sixteens are 80, and 80 with 11 more is 91.
(d) Because BCD gives each denary digit its own 4-bit group, each display digit can be driven straight from its own group, which the binary counter's single pattern cannot do.
marking_guidance: Read the given table: (a) the BCD cell completed as 1001 0001 - 1 mark, and the completed row shows the same value 91 in each representation.
Answer and values: (b) the result 1100 1010 with the reason - 202 fits in eight bits, so there is no overflow - 3 marks, one per correct entry: the sum, the fit, the reason; (c) 91 - 1 mark.
Reason: (d) the display reads its digits from the BCD store because each digit has its own group - 1 mark; the table shows the system choosing the right representation for each part.
